opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons it has to start early rather than being something you bolt on once systems are obviously dangerous.

The first is just that security is slow. You can't decide one quarter that you'd like your weights to be robust against a well-resourced state actor and then have that be true the next quarter. It involves hardware, how you structure access internally, how many people can touch the weights, insider-threat programs, and a security culture that takes years to mature. If you wait until a model is clearly capable enough that theft would be catastrophic, you're probably already too late. The capability arrives faster than the security does.

The second is that a lot of the policy and safety story depends on it. When I think about responsible scaling policies, or any regime where you say "we'll pause or add safeguards when we see certain dangerous capabilities," that commitment is only meaningful if the weights stay where you put them. If someone can exfiltrate the model, then all your careful deployment restrictions, monitoring, and refusal training don't matter much. The stolen copy can be fine-tuned, run without oversight, and used however the thief likes. Security is kind of the precondition for every other safeguard doing anything.

Third, there's a dynamic around races and proliferation. If the leading developers can't protect their weights, the frontier effectively becomes available to whoever is willing to steal it, including actors with much less interest in being careful. That makes coordination harder, because there's less reason to slow down if you think your work will just leak to someone less cautious. Good security is part of what makes it possible for careful actors to actually be the ones setting the pace.

And finally, I think there's some value in just establishing the norm while the stakes are moderate. It's much easier to get companies to accept something like "we hold ourselves to a high security standard" when it's a bit costly but not existential for their business, and it becomes the expected baseline. If you try to impose it later, under competitive pressure and with enormous economic value at stake, there's a lot more resistance.

So my overall view is that weight security is one of the less glamorous parts of AI safety, but it's quite load-bearing, and it has long lead times, which is exactly the kind of thing you want to be investing in before you're sure you need it.

r001.rationale: Says security takes years and that waiting until theft would be catastrophic means you are probably already too late.

r002.rationale: Explains that exfiltration can nullify deployment restrictions, monitoring, and refusal training, undermining other safeguards.

r003.rationale: Discusses catastrophic theft and proliferation risks, but does not identify security failures as central to many plausible catastrophic AI harm scenarios over the next couple of years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that security isn't something you can bolt on at the last minute. If you imagine a world where, in a few years, model weights are one of the most valuable and strategically important artifacts on earth, then the relevant adversaries aren't going to be random hackers, they're going to be well-resourced state actors. And getting to the point where you can actually defend against that kind of adversary is a multi-year project. It involves changing how your organization is structured, who has access to what, how your infrastructure is built, what your culture around security looks like. Those things don't change overnight.

So if you wait until the moment where the weights are obviously extremely valuable, you've already lost, because the lead time to build the kind of security you'd want is longer than the warning you're going to get. You have to start building that capacity before it's clearly necessary, which is always an awkward thing to argue for, because at the time it looks like you're spending a lot of effort on a threat that hasn't materialized yet.

There's a second reason, which is more about the dynamics between actors. A lot of the scenarios I worry about involve some kind of race, where the ability to steal weights from a leading lab means that the lab's caution doesn't actually buy anything. If a lab decides to slow down, or to put a lot of effort into alignment, or to not deploy something until they understand it, that decision only matters if other actors can't just take the model and do whatever they want with it. So security is kind of a precondition for any of the other careful behavior being meaningful. If you don't have it, then every unilateral commitment a lab makes is sort of hollow.

And then I think there's a weaker but still real point about norms and expectations. If the leading labs establish early on that this is something you take extremely seriously, that's more likely to become the baseline that everyone's held to, including by governments. Whereas if everyone's sloppy and then tries to tighten up later, you end up in a much worse equilibrium. So I'd rather see people overinvest in it now, even if in some sense it's premature, than discover that we needed it and didn't have it.

r001.rationale: It says security must be built before weights become obviously valuable and strategically important, but does not clearly state that a leak at that point would be catastrophic.

r002.rationale: It says stolen weights could nullify a lab’s caution or alignment efforts, making those safety measures hollow without security.

r003.rationale: It mentions race scenarios involving weight theft, but does not identify security failures as central to catastrophic AI harm over the next couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that security has a long lead time. If you wait until you have a model where stealing the weights would be a really big deal, you may not have time to build the systems needed to protect it. You need both technical infrastructure and an organization that’s accustomed to operating securely, and those are hard to put together quickly.

There’s also an asymmetry: once someone has copied the weights, you can’t really undo that. You can patch a vulnerability, but you can’t recall the model. And whoever has it can run it outside whatever safeguards or monitoring you’ve established.

So you want security to be improving ahead of capabilities. That doesn’t mean every model today needs the strongest imaginable protection. It means you need a credible path to protecting much more consequential models, rather than assuming you’ll figure it out when you get there.

r001.rationale: The response says security should improve ahead of capabilities and before stealing weights becomes a “really big deal,” but it does not clearly state that stronger protection must precede a leak becoming catastrophic.

r002.rationale: It says a leaked model can be run outside established safeguards or monitoring, clearly communicating that security failures can undermine other safety measures.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify security failures as central to plausible catastrophic AI harm scenarios over the next couple of years.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that security takes a long time to build, and you don’t want to start when the first model that really needs protecting is already sitting on your servers. By that point, someone may already have access to your systems. It’s much harder to get them out than to prevent them from getting in in the first place.

There’s also a potentially sharp transition in how valuable the weights are. Today, stealing a model might let you reproduce a product more cheaply. At some point, it could give you access to a system that substantially accelerates AI research or enables serious misuse. You want the security to be in place before you cross that threshold, even if you’re uncertain about exactly when it will happen.

And this matters for whether developers can make responsible decisions. If you decide a model is too dangerous to release, but someone can just steal the weights, then your decision doesn’t accomplish very much. Security is part of having the ability to say, ‘We should wait.’

r001.rationale: It says security should be in place before weights become valuable enough to enable serious misuse, capturing protection before a potentially catastrophic leak.

r002.rationale: It explains that stolen weights can defeat a decision to withhold a dangerous model, showing how a security failure can undermine a safety measure.

r003.rationale: It mentions the possibility of serious misuse but does not say security failures are central to many plausible catastrophic-harm scenarios over the next couple of years.
